title: Breaking Up with the Cloud: A Wearable That Keeps Your Secrets

content:
For the past month, my team has been busy iterating, coding, and debugging alongside our friends at the Biomedical Engineering Association (BEA). If you haven’t caught up yet, we are jointly developing a smart wristband designed to track sport and sleep metrics with a strict “local-only” data policy. While BEA handles the physical device, our team has been fully focused on the software ecosystem. We are now at a point where the concept is turning into reality, so we wanted to pause and share a concrete update on what we’ve built so far. Below, you’ll find a detailed breakdown of the current state of our firmware and the architecture behind our privacy-centric mobile app.

Firmware Development

For the hardware brain, we are utilizing the nRF52840-DK board , which runs on a powerful Cortex-M4 processor. However, power comes with constraints: we only have 1MB of flash memory to work with. This is a huge limitation that forces us to optimize every line of code; we can’t store days of history on the device itself, making the real-time link to the phone critical.

We kicked things off by deciding on the Operating System. After evaluating FreeRTOS, we ultimately decided to flash Zephyr RTOS. It proved to be the right choice, especially when we started testing our first two available sensors:

  • Gyroscope & Accelerometer: Fortunately, Zephyr already supported the drivers for this module, saving us from having to write them from scratch.
  • Sweat Sensor (GSR): Since this is an analog sensor, we didn’t need complex drivers, we just needed to configure the ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) to read the raw data.

The Operating System Logic Once we confirmed we could read the data, we had to figure out how to manage it all at once. We moved away from a basic sequential loop and implemented a robust multi-threaded architecture.

Think of it as a hierarchy of needs: we assigned every task (sensor reading, data packaging, power management) to its own thread with a specific priority level.

  • High Priority: Critical tasks, like maintaining the Bluetooth handshake, sit at the top. This ensures that even if the processor is busy crunching numbers, the device stays connected.
  • Sensor Threads: Different sensors have different sampling needs. By isolating them in separate threads, the high-frequency data from the Gyro doesn’t get bottled up waiting for the slower temperature sensor.

Finally, to tie it all together, we implemented the Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) service. This allows the board to advertise its presence, pair with a smartphone, and securely stream this prioritized data to the mobile app, which leads us perfectly into the next section.

Communication protocols and security

In a world where biometric data breaches make headlines daily, we couldn’t treat security as an afterthought. Our promise: your body’s data never leaves your control. Every heartbeat, every step, every moment of sleep: all encrypted before it leaves the band.

BLE is inherently insecure. Standard pairing mechanisms are vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle attacks, eavesdropping, and packet replay. We needed cryptographic protection that didn’t compromise the nRF52840’s brutal constraints: 1MB of flash and a coin battery power. No bloated crypto libraries. No wasteful handshakes. Every byte and every CPU cycle had to count…

And the requirements were clear:

  • Zero-knowledge architecture: Intercepted BLE packets are gibberish without session keys
  • Forward secrecy: Stealing today’s session key doesn’t compromise yesterday’s data
  • Replay attack immunity: Recording and replaying packets fails authentication
  • Battery efficiency: Minimal impact on power consumption
  • Reliability: Graceful recovery from packet loss without re-pairing

The Protocol: How Pairing and Encryption Work

Our security architecture orchestrates three cryptographic algorithms to achieve a secure and efficient communication between the band and phone.

  1. ECDH P-256 (Key Agreement): When band and phone first meet, they perform an Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Both generate public and private key pairs, exchange the public ones over Bluetooth (yes, anyone can intercept these), then each independently computes the same shared secret. The shared secret never travels over the air, and an attacker can’t reverse-engineer it even with the public keys.
    On the phone, this shared secret is immediately stored in Android Keystore or iOS Keychain, encrypted enclaves that require biometric unlock. On the band, it’s saved to NVS (Non-Volatile Storage) in protected flash. The ephemeral private keys are wiped from RAM immediately after computation. This “bonding” survives app restarts, phone reboots, even firmware updates.
  2. HKDF-SHA256 (Session Key Derivation): We never use the shared secret directly for encryption. Instead, every reconnection generates fresh random nonces on both devices, exchanges them in plaintext, and feeds them into HKDF with the stored shared secret. Out comes a brand new 128-bit session key that lives only in RAM and expires after 30 minutes. Even if an attacker extracts today’s session key from your phone’s RAM, they can’t decrypt yesterday’s workout data.
  3. AES-CCM (Authenticated Encryption): This is what actually scrambles the packets. We chose CCM mode because it’s optimized for constrained devices and does two things simultaneously: encrypts the message (confidentiality) and appends a 16-byte authentication tag (integrity). The nRF52840 has a dedicated CryptoCell-310 hardware accelerator for AES operations, making encryption nearly free in terms of CPU and power.

The Implicit Nonce Protocol

AES-CCM requires a unique nonce for every encrypted packet. Reusing a nonce catastrophically breaks the encryption. The standard approach sends the 12-byte nonce with each packet, wasteful when transmitting hundreds of packets per session.

Instead, we implemented implicit nonces. Both devices initialize a base nonce during session establishment and maintain synchronized counters in RAM. The actual nonce is constructed as:

Nonce[12 bytes] = BaseNonce[8 bytes] + Counter[4 bytes, Big Endian]

Here’s the catch: the nonce never travels over BLE. Both sides build it independently from their synchronized counters. When the phone sends packet #42, it constructs nonce #42, encrypts the data, and transmits only the ciphertext. The band builds the same nonce #42 using its own counter and decrypts. If the MAC check passes, both increment to 43. If it fails, either the packet corrupted or the counters desynced.

Lost packets break synchronization. Say packet #50 never arrives at the band. The phone’s counter is at 51, but the band’s still at 50. The next packet fails to decrypt because they’re using different nonces. Instead of giving up, we try the next 5 nonces in sequence (51, 52, 53, 54, 55). If one works, we resync and continue. This handles up to 5 consecutive packet losses. Beyond that, we force re-pairing.

Implementation: Band and App

Band

On the nRF52840, we face two constraints: 1MB of flash and coin battery power. Heavy crypto libraries like mbedTLS would consume hundreds of kilobytes. Instead, we use the chip’s built-in CryptoCell-310 hardware accelerator, a dedicated crypto chip that handles AES-CCM operations while the main processor handles sensors and BLE.

Each nonce combines a device-unique ID with the packet counter, guaranteeing nonces never collide across factory resets. After every encryption, the counter is saved to NVS asynchronously. This persistence is critical: if the band loses power mid-session, it must resume from the last saved counter.

App

On the mobile app, we built a security layer that mirrors this logic. The same ECDH key exchange, HKDF key derivation, and AES-CCM encryption. The session manager handles pairing, reconnection, retry logic, and nonce desync recovery.

The long-term shared secret lives in Android Keystore or iOS Keychain, encrypted enclaves requiring biometric unlock. Session keys exist only in RAM and expire after 30 minutes. Even if an attacker extracts today’s session key, they can’t decrypt yesterday’s data.

Achievements and trade-off

The system delivers real guarantees against replay attacks (incrementing counters), MITM attacks (both sides contribute to the shared secret), and ensures forward secrecy (stealing today’s session key won’t compromise past sessions), and by doing so, we are perfectly aligned with industry’s standards.

The implicit nonce protocol saves 12 bytes per packet, offsetting the 16-byte MAC overhead with just 4 bytes of net cost. Battery impact? Negligible, because the CryptoCell handles AES-CCM in hardware while radio transmission dominates power consumption.

Philosophy behind the choice

Building this layer reinforced a core principle: security is a system property, not a feature you add later. Every design decision (implicit nonces, hardware acceleration, retry logic, nonce desync recovery) emerged from assuming the worst. We assumed every BLE packet is intercepted. Every phone is rooted. Every attacker has infinite patience and computational power. Under those assumptions, the data still stays safe, and that’s the promise we had to deliver.

App Development

If the firmware is the nervous system capturing raw signals, the mobile app is the cortex, interpreting and storing those experiences. Built with Flutter, the application functions as a robust data vault. We engineered a strictly “local-only” pipeline where parsing, storage, and visualization execute entirely on the device, real-time, with zero cloud dependency.

Optimizing BLE Connectivity

The first challenge was handling a high-frequency stream without packet loss. We utilize flutter_blue_plus for BLE management. To eliminate accidental connections in noisy environments, we implemented Proximity Pairing. By filtering for Signal Strength (RSSI) > -70dBm, the app only “sees” the wristband when it is intentionally brought close to the phone.

Once connected, the app subscribes to the characteristic notification, opening the floodgates for real-time transmission.

The Data Pipeline

To maximize throughput and battery life, we bypass standard JSON. The firmware transmits raw binary data, an opaque, bit-packed array of 18 bytes.

We implemented parsing logic within our data handling layer, using Dart’s ByteData views to efficiently extract values.

The moment a packet is unpacked, the data is multicasted via Dart’s asynchronous streams: one stream drives the live UI graph (visualising biometric fluctuations instantly), while the other feeds the persistence layer.

Privacy-First Storage (SQLite)

To honor our privacy commitment, we integrated SQLite (via sqflite) directly into the app. However, writing every millisecond update to disk immediately would freeze the app. To solve this, we implemented Batch Inserts, queuing data in memory and committing it in chunks to keep the UI buttery smooth.

Crucially, we designed a relational schema that organizes data for future analysis:

  • Sessions Table: Organizes millions of points into discrete workouts.
  • Samples Table: Separating high-frequency motion samples allows the AI model to query from other sensor data.

This separation is key: when we later implement our AI Model, the model can query exactly the motion data it needs without churning through unrelated noise.

Privacy by Design

Our architecture reflects this promise: with no API service and no cloud sync, data begins on the wrist and ends on the phone’s encrypted disk. By keeping the logic local and the architecture simple, we ensure that biometric data remains secure and isolated.
